_about: Every field a game file may contain, laid out as a game file, with a sentence where each value would be. Keys starting with an underscore are not sections: they describe vocabularies that are not shapes. A nested block is a moment — it says when the thing inside it happens, so one word can mean one thing (needs is a gate wherever it appears, and the block says what it gates). Fields still sitting flat on a card are moments that have not moved yet, which makes this file the honest record of how far that has got. tests/integration/schema.lua asserts this file and the validator know the same fields in both directions, so if they disagree one of them is a bug.
title: string shown in the HUD. Defaults to Ravel.
seed: number fixing the RNG so shuffles and every random choice replay identically. Omit for a different game each run.

players.card: the key of the card that is this seat — a seat is a card, so it has stats, can be looked at, targeted and destroyed. Leave it out and the engine injects an invisible stat bag, which is what a solitaire game has.

stats.<stat key>: number the injected seat starts with. Only for a seat the engine makes; one that names a card takes its numbers from that card's card_stats.

players.text: the injected seat's name, shown where a card's title would be. Defaults to You.

stats.key: name cards spend and conditions read. round and plays are reserved: the engine manages them, declare them only to show them. won is reserved too and sits on every seat, 0 until a game sets it — stat_gain:won@<the winning seat>:1 is how a game with two seats says who won, and the ending screen reads it against the seat this client claimed.
stats.label: string for the HUD row. Defaults to the key.
stats.min: number the stat is clamped to below. Usually 0.
stats.max: number the stat is clamped to above.
stats.subject: a subject expression the HUD row displays instead of the plain total, while the key still names what cards spend: sum:defense@standing shows the buildings still standing.
on: tag names — whose number this is. Carrying a stat is how a card says it takes part in it: an action skips a card that has none, and an absent stat fails every comparison rather than reading as zero. Naming the cards here is how a deck of forty says that once instead of forty times. "player" is the useful one a game never types: the engine stamps it onto the cards the players list names, so a stat every seat holds — a purse, a score, a hand size — is declared here rather than copied onto each seat card and copied again when a third player is added.
stats.start: the number every card named by "on" starts with. Its own card_stats still wins, so one card may start somewhere else. Left out, the stat is one each of those cards must declare itself — "a creature has hp, and every creature says how much" — and the validator names the card that forgot. Saying start without on is refused, since it would not know whose number it is.
stats.icon: the shape drawn beside this stat's number, on a card face and in the HUD: coin, heart, shield, banner, leaf, blade, arrow, card, fist, orb, pot, diamond, or none. Named by shape rather than by meaning — what a game calls its currency is its own business — and a closed set, so a shape nobody draws is refused rather than silently becoming a diamond. Left out, it is the diamond; "none" draws no shape at all, for a badge that is only a number.
stats.color: the colour of that shape, as a palette name or #rrggbb — the same vocabulary a zone paints its squares with. Left out, the shape's own colour is used, which is what makes an undeclared stat readable. Say it when the closed set of shapes has run out before a game's numbers have: Splendor has five gems and six silhouettes to borrow from, and onyx came out an orange sword.
pays_for: other stat keys a unit of this stat may be spent as — "a plain arrow can be spent as a red one", "a gold token can be spent as any colour", "a coloured mana can be spent as generic". Said here, once, rather than on every card that might use it, so a cost stays one map of what is owed. Working out which pool settles which part of a cost is a matching, and the engine solves it by taking the most constrained demand first and its own stat before any substitute — which is exact as long as the substitution sets are nested or disjoint, and the validator refuses any other shape.
stats.number: false when the badge is the shape alone, for a stat that is a fact rather than a quantity: a banner meaning "this is an attack" wears no number, and the 1 that carries it would be noise on the card. The mirror of icon "none", which is a number with no shape.
tags: a list of words; the engine knows hidden (keep it out of the HUD while cards may still read and change it)

verbs.key: the game's own name for a moment — "damage", "poison", "heal". It is what actions write and what an aura watches, and it may not be a word the engine already has: one spelling, one meaning.
verbs.does: the engine verb that carries it, "stat_damage" or "stat_gain". **A mechanism is not a meaning.** Poison and a sword both take hp and armour stops one of them; a plane losing altitude is neither, and an action string has nowhere else for the difference to live. So a game names the moments it means and writes "poison:hp@target:1" where it means poison. The point is what it makes impossible: an aura may watch a declared verb and never an engine one, so bookkeeping written with a plain stat_damage — a combat shuffling its own counters about — can never be intercepted, because nothing is able to name it. Being interfered with is something a game opts into, moment by moment. A verb declared and never performed is reported, the same way a reaction answering a verb nothing emits is.
verbs.tooltip: what the word means, shown wherever a keyword's is — "armour does not stop poison", written once in the place the rule lives

<your name for it>.stat: the stat on the card that decides it, read from that card alone
<your name for it>.less_than: number: the tag holds while the stat is under it
<your name for it>.less_than_stat: another stat key on the same card: the tag holds while the first is under the second
<your name for it>.less_than_max: true: the tag holds while the stat is under its own declared maximum. This is "damaged", and it is what a card_stats ceiling makes expressible without a second stat standing in for it.
<your name for it>.at_least: number: the tag holds while the stat reaches it
<your name for it>.equals: number: the tag holds while the stat is exactly it

computes.key: unique name, which may never be a stat key: the amount slot reads a compute and every condition reads a stat, and one word cannot be both
computes.from: what the number is made of: "<term>", or "<term> <op> <term>" with one of + - * and spaces around it. A term is a number or a subject ("0 - health@across", "cost_white@self - b_white@mine.player"). One operator and no parentheses, so there is no precedence to remember — n-ary addition is already successive stat_gain lines onto one stat. A term may name another compute, which the ability using it must list first.
computes.tooltip: prose saying what the number means. A compute is where a rule's arithmetic is written down once and given a name, so this is the sentence that would otherwise be a comment nobody can write in JSON.

<your style name>.color: cards: [r, g, b] each 0 to 1 for the plate behind the art, or false for no plate at all — so a transparent PNG shows the board through it
<your style name>.title: cards: false draws no title, giving the whole card to the picture
<your style name>.border: cards: false draws no frame around the card. A chess piece is not a card and should not be drawn inside one; selection and eligibility outlines still draw, because those are the affordance rather than the frame.
<your style name>.fit: zones: how a card sits in the box its layout gives it. card (the default) keeps card proportions and leaves breathing room; fill takes the whole box, for board tiles and for buttons — a word you have to read is not a picture of a card. On a row it also settles the shape, since a filled row has no card ratio to lay out against: it picks the column count whose cells come out closest to square
<your style name>.fan: stack zones: show the whole stack instead of only its top card, each card laid over the one before and leaving a strip of it showing. The word is the direction the next card goes — up, down, left or right — so down is a solitaire tableau and up is a row growing away from its owner. The strip is what the layout protects: cards shrink to keep it readable rather than the other way round. Not for grid zones, which place by slot.
<your style name>.ratio: zones: the shape it keeps whatever the window is — width over height, so 1 is square, or the word grid to read it from the cell count. The zone takes the largest rect of that shape inside what pos allotted, centred.
chequer: grid zones: two colours alternated across the squares, palette names or #rrggbb. The first is the colour of a1 — the bottom-left square — and a board wanting the other way round swaps the two strings; there is no flag for it

paint.<absolute pattern name>: grid zones: a colour or a picture for the squares that pattern names — terrain, goal rows, home rows

<your style name>.cell_outline: grid zones: false draws no outline on empty cells, for a board that paints its own squares. Eligible squares still light up during a move.
badges: cards: stat keys drawn as numbers along the bottom edge of the face, left to right — ["power", "health"] is a creature card. Without it a card shows hp (with its hp_max companion) as a coloured bar's worth and nothing else, which is the default every game before this was written against. A card that carries numbers and names none of them here shows none of them.
<your style name>.badge_run: cards: which way that list runs — "right", the default, along the bottom edge, or "down" the left edge from the top corner. A column is for more numbers than go across a card: a printed price of five gems is the case that asked for it, and it is also how the card being copied prints it. A column leaves the title its full width, where a row makes way for it.
<your style name>.badge_zeros: cards: false leaves out a badge whose number is zero. A separate word from badge_run deliberately — a market card's cost of no rubies is not a line of the price, while a creature's zero power is a fact and must still draw.

cards.key: unique name. Cards, actions, conditions and scopes all reference it, and it may never collide with a zone key or a tag.
cards.text: the card title, drawn on its face
cards.tooltip: prose shown in the hover panel after a short delay. May carry two marks: *bold* for the mechanics, _italic_ for flavour, which is set a size smaller. A mark that never closes is left as the character it is, so weather_now stays one word.
cards.story: long prose for the full-screen page overlay and the detail view
cards.asset: a picture: a name in the assets table, a bare filename in games/assets, an http(s) URL, a shape spec like star:5:amber, or auto for a generated one. A name is anything with no source in it, which is what tells the five apart. A picture that cannot be produced draws a generated placeholder derived from the card key, never nothing.
tags: a list of words. Free vocabulary for targeting and counting, except where the engine knows one (see _engine_tags) or a style is named after one (see styles) — a card claims a look by tagging it.

card_stats.<stat key>: the stat each instance is created with. A number is a bare current value. A card that carries its own bounds writes them by name beside it — { "value": 4, "max": 4 }, and "min" alongside — which are the same three words the stats entry uses, so there is no order to remember. A bound left out is whatever the global stats entry declares, and none at all if it declares none, so a card writes only the one it differs on. Split at creation into the current value, its ceiling and its floor, so every reader downstream still asks for the stat by name.

cost.<stat key or sacrifice:tag>: number paid when the card is played. It gates the card and dims it when unaffordable. A scope is allowed, a measuring fn is not: counting things is asking, not spending, so count: and sum: belong in needs. One map, always: two ways to settle a cost is a fact about the stats, said with pays_for on the one that stands in.

needs: conditions gating the card without consuming anything, all of which must hold: ["gold >= 3"]. See _conditions.

target.type: card, slot or zone: what the player points at
target.min: number of targets that must be chosen
target.count: number setting min and max at once
tags: every tag a candidate must carry; computed tags count
zones: only look in these zones. A per-seat key means yours unless an owner word says otherwise.
target.fill: slots only: what may already be standing there. empty (default), enemy, open (empty or enemy), any.
moves: pattern names limiting the squares offered, written for you when the card declares moves
where: conditions asked of each candidate, with the candidate as @target and as the anchor for any pattern inside — so they can say things about the destination that fill cannot. "row@target == 1" is the near row of a grid; "count:unit@across >= 1" is a cell with something standing opposite it. See _conditions.

phases: phase key or list: this card may be played only in those. Naming none means any phase.
action: action strings run when the card is played. See _actions.
play.spent: where the card goes once its play is over, as a scope like "mine.table" or "mine.graveyard". **However it ends** — resolved, or countered before it ever ran. An MTG sorcery goes to the graveyard either way and a deck-builder's chip to the table either way, and neither the action list nor the card that countered it should be the one that remembers. Opt-in: leave it out and the action list is answerable for its own card, exactly as before. Resolved as the card's owner, so "mine" is whose card it is and not whoever happened to be acting.

cost.<stat key, sacrifice:tag, or exhaust>: number paid when the ability is used, same rules as play.cost. It may be a subject instead of a number, measured when the cost is judged — "price@self" is a shop whose buy lives on the tag its zone hands out and so cannot type a price. A compute the ability bound before it ran stands here too, which is where a price with something taken off it is said, since a compute has arithmetic a cost has no room for. "exhaust": 1 is MTG's tap symbol — the ability spends the card being ready, so it may be used once a round and a card already spent cannot pay it. An ability that does not charge it stays available. Only an activate cost may ask for it.

activate.target: the same shape as play.target, for the board ability rather than the play
phases: phase key or list: the ability works only in those. Separate from play.phases, so a card can be playable in one phase and activatable in another.
action: action strings run when the card is clicked on the board. Being spent is a cost, not a consequence: an ability exhausts its card only if its cost says so.
activate.merge: what this ability says when it meets the others on the same card. "both" (the default) adds it to whatever else the card can do and the player is asked which — a rook lying in a discard pile can be taken *and* still moved. "this" is mine alone: everything else the card offers goes quiet, which is what a shop wants, since a chip lying in the bank is merchandise and its own ability paying out on a click is money from the shop window. "other" is the understudy — mine only when the card offers nothing else. Written on the ability rather than on the zone that granted it, because a card's own tag needs the same word: "this card's abilities do not work" is the same conflict with no zone in it. Two abilities claiming "this" is a contradiction the validator refuses.
moves: how a piece moves on a grid: a pattern name on its own, or a rule shaped like the one beside it. Declaring this writes the activate target for you, so clicking the piece opens targeting.

patterns: the direction sets this rule moves by, named under "patterns". Several means the union of them.
moves.fill: what may already be standing on a square this rule offers: empty (the default), enemy, open (empty or enemy), any. It knows only what is there, never anything else about it.
needs: conditions asked once for the whole rule, about the piece rather than about any square — "has this king moved yet". It cannot tell one candidate from another; that is what where is for.
where: conditions asked once per candidate square, with that square as @target and as the anchor for any pattern inside it. En passant and castling are written here, and because every question is relative the same rule serves both sides of the board.

abilities.key: a name for this ability, unique on the card
abilities.text: what it does, in the player's words. This is the label in the chooser, so a card with more than one ability needs it.
abilities.tooltip: the long version, shown on hover. The text above is a label and should stay short enough to read at a glance.
abilities.asset: the picture for this ability's entry in the chooser. Naming an entry from the assets section works as anywhere else, so one with a picture per player wears the colours of whoever opened the chooser. Without it the engine draws a shape derived from the ability's name.

cost.<stat key, sacrifice:tag, or exhaust>: paid when this ability is used, not when another is

abilities.target: the same shape as play.target, for this ability alone
phases: phase key or list: this ability works only in those
compute: compute keys, worked out in this order before the ability is judged and again before it runs. Each sees the ones before it, which is the whole of the dependency rule. Their names then stand as amounts in the actions below and as operands in the when above.
when: conditions deciding whether this ability happens at all. Unlike phases and cost — which say whether a *player* may use it — this is part of the rule: "damage past the blocker" is a sentence with an if in it, and a phase running the zone honours it too. Without it the only way to write the if is multiplying by a stat that is 0 or 1.
action: what this ability does. @self is the card carrying it, even when a chooser was shown in between.
abilities.merge: what this ability says when it meets the others on the same card. "both" (the default) adds it to whatever else the card can do and the player is asked which — a rook lying in a discard pile can be taken *and* still moved. "this" is mine alone: everything else the card offers goes quiet, which is what a shop wants, since a chip lying in the bank is merchandise and its own ability paying out on a click is money from the shop window. "other" is the understudy — mine only when the card offers nothing else. Written on the ability rather than on the zone that granted it, because a card's own tag needs the same word: "this card's abilities do not work" is the same conflict with no zone in it. Two abilities claiming "this" is a contradiction the validator refuses.
moves: how a piece moves, if this ability is a move

reactions.to: the verb this reaction answers: "play", "activate", or any verb an emit: action raises ("summon", "crash", "buy"). The card acted on never names what answers it — it emits a self-describing event carrying its own tags, and a reaction says which events it wants. That is what stops a fireball having to list every counter to it.
where: conditions over the event's subject, read through @event — the card that was played, activated or emitted about. This is where a reduced reaction is written: "tagged:fireball@event >= 1" answers only fireballs, "value@event <= 3" answers a crash of three or less but not a four. The one condition grammar, nothing bespoke.
so the same card answers a summon with one reaction and a fireball with another, and neither with the other's.
when: conditions over the reacting card's own state — whether it can be afforded or is legal now. About the reactor, where "where" is about the event and a play's "needs" is about the player.
reactions.whose: whose announcement this may answer, in the words a scope already uses: "enemy" (somebody else's — the default, and what every reaction meant before this field existed), "mine" (your own, and only your own — Magic answering your own spell on the stack), or "anyone". A word rather than a flag because three readings do not fit in a yes or no. The seat that announced is asked first when it applies, since it is already holding priority. Nothing loops: one card answers one record once, and an answer is a new record with its own memory, so a chain gets longer rather than going round.
reactions.forced: "optional" (default: the controller is prompted and may decline) or "mandatory" (it fires on its own — Magic's mandatory triggered ability). Not a boolean, because "you may" and "it must" are both triggered abilities and the difference is the whole of what this says.
reactions.from: where answering happens from, which decides what it does: "hand" plays the reaction as a card (it goes on the stack and resolves), "board" activates or fires a card already in play (the card stays, its effect stacks), or **a zone by name** for the third shape — a row of ongoing effects laid face up in front of one player is in play and is a *hand* as far as a zone type goes, and guessing which face-up zones count as in play gets a discard pile wrong. Left out, the zone the card sits in decides.

cost.<stat key, sacrifice:tag, or exhaust>: paid by the reactor when it answers, out of their own pool — priority makes "mine" the reactor for the duration

reactions.target: the same shape as play.target, if answering asks the reactor to choose
action: what the reaction does. @event is what it answers; @self is the reacting card. To stop the thing reacted to, say "counterspell" — "destroy:event" reaches the card the event is about, which is rarely the same thing.
reactions.spent: where the reacting card goes once the answer is over, the same word and the same rules as play.spent. A reaction is never moved by being played, so a card that does not say this stays where it was and may answer the next announcement.
moves: how a piece moves, if this reaction is a move
compute: compute keys bound before the reaction is judged and again before it runs, as on an ability
reactions.key: a name for this reaction, unique on the card
reactions.text: what it does, in the player's words — the label when the reactor is offered a choice of several
reactions.tooltip: the long version, shown on hover

emits.play: the verb playing this card announces, or a list of them — and announcing is what makes the play answerable. A card that emits nothing plays the instant it is clicked, as every card always has; one emitting "cast" goes onto the stack zone instead and happens only once nobody has answered. The suppression is automatic: with no reaction to the verb anywhere in the game, or none the other seat could play right now, the card resolves at once and nothing is put up. Almost always written on a *tag* rather than here — one "spell" tag makes every spell in the game castable, instead of a line on each of ninety cards.
emits.activate: the verb using this card's ability announces, the same way. Kept apart from "play" because one card is often both: a spell cast from hand that resolves onto the board and is used from there is answered as two different things, and a reaction watching for one must not catch the other. What goes on the stack differs to match — a card played is put up itself, a card activated stays where it lies and its effect goes up on an event standing for it, so "self" in the deferred action is still the card.

cards.menu_for: engine-written, never authored: marks the card the engine generates to stand for one ability in a chooser. A card with several abilities gets one per ability, labelled with the ability's text and drawn with a shape generated from its name.

needs: conditions deciding pass from fail. Unlike the blocks around it this is not a moment but a named test: any action list reaches it by running resolve_challenge, so one challenge can be asked from play and from activate both, which is what a crisis card that stays on the board when it fails needs.
pass: action strings run when the condition holds
fail: action strings run when it does not

needs: conditions deciding whether the card being played may be sent to THIS card, with itself as @self and the arriving card as @target. Same shape again; asked of the destination.
action: action strings run when a card lands here, with this card as @self and the newcomer as @target. What the destination does about an arrival, said once by the destination rather than by every card that might arrive.
action strings run at each round boundary while the card is on a grid and not ruined

leaves.into: the zone this card landed in, and the whole of what tells one kind of leaving from another: the discard is a death, a trash is an exile, "hand" is a bounce. The engine learns none of those names. Leave it out and the block answers any departure.
action: action strings run when this card leaves play — out of a zone whose status is "board" into one that is not, with @self as the departing card. Moving between two board zones is not leaving anything. Written on a tag it covers a whole class at once, which is how "every unit announces its death" is one line; a tag hands it over whole and a card writing its own takes none of the tag's, the same rule play keeps. destroy: does NOT fire it — a destroyed card lands in no zone, so there is no "into" to name, and its stats are cleared, so a rule running afterwards has nothing left to read. A removal you want answered is a move into a zone.

where: conditions deciding which of the revealed cards may be picked, asked of each with the candidate as @target and this card as @self — the same word and the same vocabulary a target's "where" uses. The whole scope still comes up, because revealing a hand is usually half the rule; only the cards that qualify can be clicked. "Largest" is a comparison with the offer itself: "sum:value@target >= max:value@options". An offer where nothing qualifies does not open at all, since a mandatory question with no answer never closes. Only cards show: *borrowed* are asked — an entry options: dealt came off this card's own list, and narrowing a list you wrote is writing a shorter list.
action: action strings run when somebody picks a card out of the offer this card opened with show:. The pick is @target and this card is @self, which is the reverse of an options: offer — there the entry carries the rule, here the entry is somebody else's property and carries nothing of ours.

cards.outcome: "victory" or "defeat" on an ending card, which gives a banner, a run summary and a flourish. It is a word about the only player there is, so a game with two seats says who won by setting the reserved "won" stat on a seat instead, and needs no field here

zones.key: unique name, which may never collide with a card key or any tag. Some names are load-bearing: hand, graveyard, board, reveal and system have engine meanings a game may override by declaring them.
zones.label: string drawn on the zone
zones.layout: where the cards are drawn: stack (one on top of another, so only the top of the pile shows), row (side by side, each showing its text, wrapping onto more lines rather than shrinking when one line would be too tight — add "row": "down" or "right" to overlap them into a fan that still reads down its whole length), grid (addressed cells, which is what "grid": [cols, rows] is for and the only layout with a capacity), or page (each card fills the zone, for a story panel).
zones.visibility: who may read the cards here — a drawing question and nothing else, so a card in play may be unreadable and a card nobody can touch may be plain to see. "public" is everyone, "owner" is the seat whose zone it is (a zone with no seat is nobody's secret, so it stays public), "secret" is nobody — backs out, and a stack's order is scrambled in the browser because the order is the secret and the contents usually are not. Default public.
zones.reach: which of the cards here exist as far as the rules go: "all", or "top" — only the last one, which is what a stack means and is its default. A row can say "top" too: a column of cards fanned so every one is readable while only the last is in play is exactly Lost Cities' expedition.
zones.use: what may be done with a card lying here at all — the ceiling, which a phase's "zone" then narrows: playing needs both to agree. "play" (default), "abilities" (its own activate blocks work here, which is what a board means), or "none" — a box you use rather than reach into, and the only way to say that a trash or an exile is untouchable. Cards nobody can see default to "none", which is what makes a deck a deck.
zones.display: "onscreen" (default) or "offscreen" — not drawn, and nothing in it clickable. For offers, fate decks and rules pages. Different from a secret visibility, which is a zone you can see and cannot read.
zones.copies: "one" (default) or "per_seat" — one zone each, and "pos" then takes one rect per seat.
zones.status: what standing a card lying here has in the rules, which is a different question from what the zone looks like. "board" is in play — a bare tag scope, count:, card:, tagged:, sacrifice:, on_turn and a reaction answered "from": "board" all mean it. "offer" is a card lent to a question: nobody's while it is there, and gone when the question is answered. "supply" is stock — a shop's shelves, a bank of tokens, the box a game deals from: visible and countable, but nobody's and not in play, and its cards are **interchangeable**. That last word is the whole of it. Sixty-four identical gems differ in nothing a rule may ask about, so the engine keeps one of each as a real card and a number for the rest, stamped on it as "stock" — the game file writes "contents": ["gem:64"] and never learns it did not get sixty-four cards. Safe only because nothing may target one, so nothing can tell the copies apart. Filling a supply raises the number instead of minting a card; taking from one is a "stock@self" cost beside a "fill:<somewhere>:@self", never a draw, since a draw would move the card standing for the whole stock. An empty shelf keeps its card, which is what lets a game count how many stacks have run out — an absence carries no tag. "reach" and "refill_from" are refused there: a stock has no order to have a top or to run out in. "exile" is everything else — a deck, a discard, a bag, a trash — and is the default, so a zone is inert until it says otherwise. Cards in an exiled zone are still nameable, since naming a zone reaches it; what they are not is counted, sacrificed or asked to act. A grid is "board" and an options zone is "offer" without saying so, which is how a row of face-up ongoing effects says it is in play while staying a row.
zones.pos: [x1, y1, x2, y2] as fractions of the window. Per-seat zones take one such list per seat instead, which is the only place a nested array is allowed outside a pattern's vectors. Each type has a default spot; hidden zones default off-screen, which is what gives dealt cards their fly-in.
zones.grid: [cols, rows]. Legal only where "layout" is "grid" — a value names its own parameter field, which is why every word on every one of these fields is reserved against being used as a field name for anything else.
zones.row: which way a row fans, so every card in it can be read at once: "down" or "right". Legal only where "layout" is "row"; left out, the cards sit side by side and do not overlap.
contents: starting cards, each key or key:count
zones.refill_from: the key of the zone this one is rebuilt from the moment its last card leaves — a deckbuilder's draw pile naming its discard. Everything there moves in and the pile is shuffled. Per-seat zones take the same seat's copy, so one line serves every player. Asked for rather than fired on emptying: the pile refills when something tries to draw from it and finds it empty, which is when a player would pick the discard up and shake it — so the loop closes wherever it runs out, mid-draw, mid-action, inside a card that draws four. A rule that empties the pile on purpose is left alone.
applies: tags this zone hands to whatever lies in it, behaviour included. This is how a pile grants an ability no card knows about.

needs: conditions deciding whether a card being played may be sent here. Same shape as a card's accepts, asked of the zone.
action: action strings run when a card lands in this zone, with the zone as @self and the newcomer as @target. A discard pile anybody may take from says "set_owner:target:none" here, rather than every card that might be thrown into it saying it.

zones.tooltip: prose shown when the zone is hovered. A deck answers for itself — there are no cards in it to ask, only a deck — so this is what a player reads before clicking it.

cost.<stat key>: number paid to use the zone's own ability

phases: phase keys it works in. Naming none means any.
action: what clicking the zone does. This is how a deck is drawn from: the box answers, rather than the card on top of it becoming clickable.
activate.target: a target spec, the same shape as a card's play.target
moves: pattern names, if the ability is a move

zones.asset: a picture behind the whole zone, stretched to its rect. Same five forms as a card's asset.
tags: a list of words; the engine knows several for zones (see _engine_tags), and a zone claims a look by naming a style (see styles)

phases.key: unique name. A phase key must never name a seat: both players share one play phase, and seat: next is what makes the turn theirs.
phases.label: string for the HUD
phases.type: automatic (run actions once and advance), player_input (play freely), draw_and_play (player_input with ends_after 1 and discard_hand), or overlay (dim the screen, deal into its zone, and resolve by *playing* one of the cards dealt — choosing is playing. Push-only, and a choice costs nothing: cost, needs and targeting are skipped)
actions: action strings run when the phase begins — any phase, not only automatic ones. On a phase that hands over, the seat has already changed, so "mine" is the player about to act.
phases.deck: zone key to deal from on fresh entry
phases.draw: number of cards dealt on fresh entry
phases.zone: a zone key, or a list of them. Naming it bounds what may be played to the cards in those zones; a phase naming none lets any reachable card be played, which is what the menu relies on. The FIRST is where cards are dealt and what an overlay offers, because those are singular questions — a list is a player holding two hands, an open one beside a closed one.
phases.pass_card: a card key or a list of them, dealt with every hand so a forced play always has an out
phases.ends_after: number of plays after which the phase advances itself. It counts plays and cannot tell one from another; use ends_when when only some of them should end the turn.
phases.ends_when: a condition, asked every time the game comes to rest — after every action, not only after a play. When it holds the phase advances itself. One phase says one or the other, never both, and only a phase a player acts in: automatic and overlay phases end themselves.
phases.seat: next hands over to the following seat on entry, which is the whole of turn-taking. A route may overrule it — see next.seat.
on_enter: action strings run when the turn *begins* here, as against "actions", which run every time the phase is entered. A turn begins on an arrival from another phase, and on a loop that hands the turn on — both are the same moment, and a draft that passes round the table by looping must not skip it. What it is not is a loop that keeps the same player, which is the case the split exists for: a counter reset belongs here, since running it again on the way round would undo the turn it was counting, and a number recomputed from the board belongs in "actions". Runs after the seat has moved, so "mine" is the player about to act, and before "actions". A phase nothing leads back to has only one kind of entry, and writing on_enter on one is refused.

emits.begin: the verb this phase announces when it begins, or a list of them — beside "actions", which is what it *does* when it begins. Announcing is what makes a moment answerable, and a phase was the one moment nothing could announce: a turn beginning caused nothing, so "at the start of your turn" had nowhere to be said and every rule that wanted it settled for a worse moment. The subject is the player card of whoever the phase belongs to, so a reaction reads @event as whose turn it is and "whose": "mine" means what it means everywhere else. Nothing is deferred — a phase has no action list waiting on the answer — so the announcement goes up, the phase carries on, and whatever answers resolves beside it.
emits.end: the verb this phase announces as it hands over, the same way. This is "at the end of your turn": written on the last phase of a turn, it is the moment a chip that pays out at end of turn has been waiting for. It fires as the phase leaves, beside the hand it discards, so a reaction to it acts once that phase is over.

next.when: the condition deciding whether this route is taken, written as one string — "count:king@taken >= 1". One comparison, a subject on the left and a number or another subject on the right. See _conditions.
zone_empty: zone keys that must all be empty for this route to be taken
next.then: phase key to go to. An entry with no condition always matches, and the first match wins.
next.ends_round: true ticks the round here: the counter rises, exhausted cards ready, and every card's turn action runs. Nothing else does this, and it is never inferred from list position.
next.seat: next or same, overruling the phase's own seat for this transition. It exists for the phase that leads back to itself, which different games ask opposite things of: a turn that carries on until the player is done says same, a draft passing round the table says next. Without it each of those needed two phase keys, the second a copy of the first with one word missing.

tags: a list of words; the engine knows discard_hand (leaving discards the unplayed hand, and tokens vanish) and keep_hand (a draw_and_play phase opting out of it)

end_conditions.when: the condition deciding whether the game is over, written as one string — "nexus@south_side <= 0". See _conditions.
zone_empty: zone keys that must all be empty
then: action strings run when it fires, usually push_phase to an ending overlay
end_conditions.fired: engine bookkeeping: each condition fires once per game, first match wins, and open overlays are waited for

place.card: the key of a card that starts already in play — a throne, a board, a button, a chess piece
place.owner: the key of the player this piece belongs to. Ownership is decided where a piece is put down, which is here; without it a card belongs to the seat of the zone it sits in, which is enough for per-seat tableaus. It is what lets one card be placed for both players.
place.zone: where it goes. Leave it out and its home tag decides, then the only board. A per-seat zone gets one copy in each seat's.
place.at: the square, named the way a player would say it — a column letter and a rank counted from the near edge, "e1". A list places one card per square, so eight pawns are one entry. Grid zones only; without it the card takes the first free cell.

<your tag name>.zone: the home zone of every card carrying this tag, so a move_to with no zone, a gain, and a card whose start block names none all know where it goes without saying so

buffs.<stat key>: number every card wearing this tag reads that stat higher by, for as long as it wears it — negative to read it lower. **Nothing is written to the card.** The shift is worked out on every read, so it arrives and leaves with the tag and there is no stored number to get out of step: this is a continuous effect, said once, instead of a stat_gain that whoever removes the tag has to remember to undo on every path it can leave by. The three tag sources all count, so the shift can come from what a card *is* (a printed keyword), from where it *stands* (a zone's applies — the whole of "+1 while it is in the arena"), or from how it *is doing* (a computed tag — "+2 while damaged"). That last one is the single exception to a computed tag carrying nothing: a buff is a property of wearing the word, as a style is, and there is no card for the behaviour version of it to belong to — so a computed tag may write "buffs" and nothing else. A write addresses the card's own number and a read sees the whole, so a card set to "attack 2" is printed at 2 and still reads 3 while something is granting it +1 — a level-up cannot eat a bonus it has never heard of. **The ceiling rises with the value and the floor stays**, which is what makes a 1/1 handed +1 hp a 2/2 that dies to two rather than a 1/1 that was clamped back on the spot; damage comes off the buffed total, and when the tag goes what is left is the printed number with the wound still on it. The amount is a plain number, never a subject: anything worked out belongs in a compute. A buff that leads back to itself — a computed tag shifting the stat that decides whether it holds — is refused rather than resolved, since the shift would have to know its own answer.

adjusts.key: a name for this adjustment, unique on the card, so two of them can be told apart
adjusts.verb: the **declared** verb it watches — a key from the top-level "verbs", never an engine action. See verbs.does for why that rule is the whole of the word.
adjusts.stat: which number it changes. "damage" to hp is not "damage" to gold, and a shield that stopped both would be a bug in every game that had one.
adjusts.covers: who it is about, as a scope read from the card holding it. "self" is a keyword and the fast path; "each.mine.unit" is the anthem that covers a side. The aura works only while its card is in play, as a tag scope already means.
when: conditions, in the one grammar. @self is the card holding the aura, @target the card being acted on, and @source the card doing it — which is how "takes 2 less from spells" is said.
adjusts.by: how much it shifts what lands, in the ordinary amount grammar. It adjusts the number the *action says*, as a player reads it: "3 damage" less one is 2, and the author never sees that the delta is carried negative inside. Adjustments sum, in a fixed order. **They may not change the sign** — three damage reduced by five is none, never a heal of two — because a word that could turn harm into help by accident is a word nobody can reason about. Asked before the change, so it reads the board as it was: "takes one less while damaged" sees the hp this damage has not yet come off.

play.cost: what playing one of these cards costs
play.target: a target spec for it, the same shape as a card's play.target
action: what playing one of these cards does. Two readings, and both are live. A tag a *card* carries hands the whole moment to every card wearing it — ninety Splendor development cards buy the same way, so the game says it once instead of ninety templates each keeping a copy in step. A tag a *zone* hands out with applies says what playing a card that lies *there* does, which is how an offer says what choosing from it means when the cards it deals already do something else from a hand. Whole block or none: a card writing its own play takes none of the tag's, since half a moment — the tag's action under the card's own cost — reads as cleverness and debugs as neither. Two tags granting it is refused rather than resolved, and the card does neither: which one won would be the order somebody typed the tags.

action strings this tag gives its cards — to every card carrying the tag as a keyword, and to whatever lies in a zone that hands the tag out with applies. A card is asked for its own abilities first, then its zone's, then its tags', so a keyword that changes an outcome runs after the outcome.
activate.target: a target spec for that ability, the same shape as a card's play.target
phases: phase keys the ability works in
moves: pattern names, if the ability is a move

several activated abilities instead of one, exactly as on a card. A tag that grants abilities *adds* them to whatever the card can already do.

<your tag name>.leaves: the same block a card may write for itself, handed to every card carrying this tag — "every unit of ours announces its death" is one line here and one per card everywhere else. Whole block or none, as with play.

emits.play: the verb every card carrying this tag announces when it is played — the same field a card may write for itself, and the place it belongs. "spell": { "emits": { "play": "cast" } } says once that spells go up to be answered, and every spell in the game inherits it; a Burst spell that cannot be responded to simply does not carry the tag. A zone handing the tag out through "applies" says instead that playing a card from *there* announces itself, which is how a bank makes buying answerable without the chips knowing. Written beside the moment blocks and not inside "play", on purpose: a "play" block is granted whole or not at all, so a tag that wanted only to add an announcement would take the card's own play action away from it.
emits.activate: the verb every card carrying this tag announces when its ability is used. The same tag may say both, and a card may take one word from one tag and the other from another — a "creature" that summons on play and a "tap" keyword that announces its use are two sentences about the same card, and neither has to know about the other.

<your tag name>.tooltip: what this tag means, in one place. Two readings, and both are live: a tag a *zone* hands out through "applies" describes what lying there lets a card do, and a tag a *card* carries is a keyword — the game says once what Tough does and every card with the tag inherits the sentence, in the hover panel and in the detail overlay. A card's own tooltip is shown as well, because they describe different things.

<your effect name>.base: one of damage, bleed, power_up, sparkle, stars, heal, smoke, explosion
<your effect name>.size: number multiplying the base size, default 1
<your effect name>.speed: number multiplying the base speed, default 1
<your effect name>.count: number multiplying how many particles, default 1
<your effect name>.color: [r, g, b] each 0 to 1, defaulting per base

vectors: [dx, dy] pairs, every direction written out. x is the column and y is a rank — [0,1] is one square forward, up the board — and the engine flips it for a seat sitting at the other side. When the class says absolute these are squares instead, named the way a player says them: "e1".
class: how the vectors are walked: step (once, the default), ray (repeat until stopped), ray:n (up to n times), phasing (nothing on the way stops it), absolute (the entries are squares, not directions, and the walking words mean nothing beside it)
<your pattern name>.zone: the board an absolute pattern names squares on. Relative patterns need none: they are anchored on the moving card.

<your picture name>.src: the picture itself: a bare filename in games/assets, an http(s) URL, or a shape spec. Everything a card can spell out inline is legal here. A list gives one picture per player, chosen by whose card it is — which is how one card can be a piece in either colour.
<your picture name>.max: number, 1 to 4092: the longest edge in pixels the browser hands over. Bigger pictures are scaled to it. Anything spelled out inline instead of named gets 1024.

_conditions._what: One vocabulary, used by every needs (a card's, a challenge's, a zone's receive), accepts, a phase's next entries and end_conditions. A subject is a stat key, count:<tag>, card:<key>, sum:<subject>, max:<subject> or min:<subject>, optionally carrying a scope after an @.
_conditions._yes_no: tagged:<tag> and not_tagged:<tag> answer a yes/no about a scope, as 1 or 0: "tagged:pawn@behind >= 1" is "there is a pawn there". Prefer them to counting to one; count: is for when the number is the point. An empty scope has nothing tagged, so it answers no to the first and yes to the second.
_conditions._saved: saved:<slot> is the same yes/no shape asked of the machine rather than of any card: 1 when that save slot holds a game, 0 when it does not — which is how a menu offers Continue only when there is something to continue. A build with no save layer in it answers 0, which is true there.
_conditions._form: One comparison, written as one string: <subject> <op> <number-or-subject>. The operators are >=, <=, >, <, == and !=, one per string. There are no boolean operators and no arithmetic: a list already means and, and or is two abilities.
_conditions._where_they_go: A needs, an accepts and a target's where each take a LIST of them, all of which must hold — a list rather than a map keyed by its subject, because such a map cannot name one subject twice, and "gold >= 3" with "gold <= 8" is a range. A routing entry and an end condition take exactly one, under the key when.
_conditions._measured_against_a_subject: The right-hand side may be another subject rather than a constant: "value@target >= max:value@mine.red". It must LOOK like a subject — name a scope or a measuring fn — or it is refused as a bare word, which would otherwise read as a stat worth nothing and quietly pass.
_conditions._absent_is_not_zero: A stat nobody carries fails every comparison, equals 0 included, because otherwise a gate opens exactly when the thing it guards stops existing. The measuring forms are exempt: count: and card: over nothing really is zero, and sum:/max: are asked of a pool, whose empty measure is honestly 0. min: is NOT exempt — a pool with nothing in it has no smallest member, and answering 0 would put one below every real value.
_conditions._a_cost_is_not_one: A cost stays a map of subject to number — { "gold": 2 } — because a cost is what gets SPENT, and "mana >= 3" says what to check rather than what to take away.
_conditions._scopes: After the @, [<quantifier>.][<owner>.]<name>[.<tag>], where the name is a zone key, a tag, a movement pattern, or one of self, target, all, everywhere, reach. No scope at all means your own cards. A tag scope means cards in play, on grid zones — name the zone when a single hand is what you meant, or everywhere when you mean all of them at once. A zone key may be narrowed by a tag written after it: "count:purple@enemy.hand" is the purples in one hand, which is the search a bare tag refuses to do. It narrows left to right, widest first — whose, where, which — and is the same pair a target spec writes as "zones" beside "tags". Both halves must exist: a zone that is not there answers nothing rather than falling back to the tag alone, since a typo must not quietly widen the search.
_conditions._everywhere: everywhere is every card, in whatever zone it sits — a hand, a deck, a pile or the board. It is the deliberate opposite of a bare tag, which sees the board alone so that a rule cannot read a hand it cannot see; reach for it only when you genuinely mean a tag counted wherever the card is and cannot name every zone one at a time ("count:gem@mine.everywhere" is one seat's gems in play, in hand and in the bag at once). Naming a single zone already reaches a hand, a pile or a deck; this is for all of them together. The owner word narrows it as anywhere else, so a card in a shared zone is nobody's and drops out of both mine and enemy. Distinct from all, which is every entity of every kind.
_conditions._reach: reach is the squares a set of pieces could move onto right now, answered as the things standing on them — computed from the moves each piece declares, never stored. The owner word picks whose pieces are asked, not what comes back, so "count:king@enemy.reach == 0" is "not in check". The engine has no notion of an attack: a piece may only land on an occupied square if its own move says so, so the game file has already drawn the line between moving and threatening. A move rule's own needs may not usefully ask for it — that is reach asking itself, and the circle names nothing.
_conditions._owner_of: owner_of.<scope> is the seats owning what the rest of it names, answered as their own cards: score@owner_of.target is the score of whoever owns the card the player chose, which no other scope can say — mine and enemy are relative to whoever is up, and a seat key reaches its card only because the file tagged it with its own name. What follows the prefix is an ordinary scope expression. On its own, @owner_of is the acting card's own seat. An owner word means whichever side of the prefix it stands on: inside it picks the cards (@owner_of.enemy.creature), before it it filters the seats that come back (@mine.owner_of.target). Each seat answers once however many cards it owns, and a card nobody owns names nobody.
_conditions._owners: mine (the seat whose turn it is), enemy (any other seat), anyone (no filter, said deliberately). A card's owner is the seat of the zone it sits in, or the seat whose key it carries as a tag.
_conditions._quantifiers: any (default: the pool reaches n), each (every member does, and an empty scope is false rather than vacuously true), random (as any, but one member is chosen by the seeded shuffle).

_actions._what: Colon-separated strings, run from a card's play, activate and turn actions, a challenge's pass and fail, a zone's own activate action, a phase's actions, and an end condition's then. An unknown op logs and is skipped. A numeric slot takes a number or a measuring fn, optionally multiplied by a second with :x:. A zone slot takes a scope expression too.
_actions.fill: fill:<zone>:<card>:<n> — create n instances of a card in a zone. The card slot takes a template key, or "@<scope>" to read the template off a card already lying somewhere: "fill:mine.discard:@self:1" is a shop selling what it is, where the ability lives on the tag its zone hands out and so cannot name a key. Not a clone — what arrives is a fresh card off the template, with the stats the game declared and no memory of the one that named it. Every card in scope contributes its n.
_actions.draw_from: draw_from:<from>:<to>:<n>[:top|bottom] — move n cards off the top of one zone into another. "draw_from:bag:bag:1:bottom" is how the top card of a deck is buried under it. The last argument is where in the destination it lands: "top" (the default) or "bottom". Every zone is a list and the top of a pile is its end, so this only reads as anything in a deck — but that is where burying a card is a rule rather than a detail.
_actions.return_to: return_to:<from>:<to>[:top|bottom] — move all of them, bounded so a refilling zone is safe. The destination may be the word origin, sending each card back to the square, or failing that the zone, it was in before its last move — a different place for every card, which is what empties a combat zone in one line. The last argument is where in the destination it lands: "top" (the default) or "bottom". Every zone is a list and the top of a pile is its end, so this only reads as anything in a deck — but that is where burying a card is a rule rather than a detail.
_actions.move_to: move_to[:<zone>][:<on_occupied>] — move the acting card. With no zone its home tag decides; the word target means the zone or slot the player chose; the word origin means the zone it was in before its last move, which is not the same as its home; a third part says what becomes of a piece already standing there, either destroy or the zone it goes to, and leaving it out makes an occupied square refuse the move. That third part is capture.
_actions.add_to: add_to:<zone>[:top|bottom] — move the acting card, for overlay picks. The last argument is where in the destination it lands: "top" (the default) or "bottom". Every zone is a list and the top of a pile is its end, so this only reads as anything in a deck — but that is where burying a card is a rule rather than a detail.
_actions.move_target_to: move_target_to:<zone>[:top|bottom] — move each targeted card there, or to the word origin, which sends each one back to the zone it was in before its last move. The last argument is where in the destination it lands: "top" (the default) or "bottom". Every zone is a list and the top of a pile is its end, so this only reads as anything in a deck — but that is where burying a card is a rule rather than a detail.
_actions.place: place:<scope>:<where> — put every card in scope on a square. <where> is a square by name ("g1"), or the name of a pattern pointing at one from the acting card ("one_left") — which is how a rule that works for both sides of a board says where something goes, since a named square is only ever one player's.
_actions.gain: gain:<card>:<n> — create n instances in their home zone, or the hand when no tag names one
_actions.stat_gain: stat_gain:<subject>:<n> — raise a stat, held between its floor and its ceiling, and logged. The subject may carry a scope: hp@target, hp@each.follower.
_actions.stat_damage: stat_damage:<subject>:<n> — lower it, same rules. The same arithmetic as stat_gain with the sign turned round, and a separate word because "damage 2" and "gain -2" are the same instruction to the engine and different sentences to everyone else.
_actions.stat_boost: stat_boost:<subject>:<n> — move the *ceiling*, for a card that carries one (card_stats written { "value": n, "max": n }). The current value comes with it only where it has to: a ceiling lowered under the number standing there would otherwise leave a stat above its own maximum. A stat with no declared ceiling has nothing to boost.
_actions.stat_set: stat_set:<subject>:<n> — set it directly, past every bound and without logging. An authoring tool rather than a game rule: it is how a phase resets a counter.
_actions.attach_to_target: attach_to_target — tuck the acting card under the first target
_actions.transform: transform:<scope>:<card> — replace each card in scope with a new one of that key, standing on the same square, in the same zone, belonging to the same player. Everything else is the new card's own, because it is a different card. A pawn promoting, a checker being crowned, a unit levelling up and a tile turned face up are all this.
_actions.copy: copy:<scope>[:play|activate[:<n>]] — every card the scope names does what it does, n times over, without being played and without moving. The card is not copied, its effects are: nothing is created, nothing is spent, no cost is paid, and the card stays where it lies — which is what "play it twice, then trash it" means and what duplicating the card would get wrong. The moment says which of its two action lists to run, "play" (the default) or "activate" (the first ability it offers). The copied card is the one acting, so its action reads @self as itself; targets are not carried over, since nobody aimed the copy — a card meant to be copied should say what it acts on rather than wait to be pointed at something.
_actions.destroy: destroy:<scope>[:<n>] — remove those cards from play entirely. A bare zone key is a scope, so destroy:hand still works. The count says how many of them, and takes the same amount grammar as any other ("sum:crashed@enemy.player", "count:gem", a plain number) — which is what "trash three of these" needs and writing the line three times cannot give, since how many is usually known only as the game runs. Which ones: the earliest, unless the scope says "random", because most pools are identical cards and spending randomness on a choice that does not matter costs a reproducible game for nothing. Left out, the count is every card the scope names — except after "random", which means one. **It triggers nothing.** A destroyed card lands in no zone, so a "leaves" block has no "into" to name, and its stats are cleared with it, so a rule running afterwards would have nothing left to read. That is what this verb is for — taking something off the table that nobody may ask about. A removal you want answered is a move into a zone.
_actions.set_owner: set_owner:<scope>:<who> — hand those cards to a seat, to the one that is up ("mine"), or to nobody ("none"). Whose a card is is decided when it is dealt and stays decided, so this is the only thing that changes it: mind control, and a pile that disowns whatever lands in it. Seats are numbered from 1 and nobody is 0.
_actions.move: move:<scope>:<zone>[:top|bottom] — every card the scope names goes to that zone, or to the word origin, which sends each one back to the zone it was in before its last move. The scope-first sibling of move_to (the acting card) and move_target_to (the ones a player chose), for a set nobody picked: "move:mine.battle:mine.bench" sends the survivors home, and writing it again with enemy covers the other seat without asking whose turn it is. The last argument is where in the destination it lands: "top" (the default) or "bottom". Every zone is a list and the top of a pile is its end, so this only reads as anything in a deck — but that is where burying a card is a rule rather than a detail.
_actions.activate_zone: activate_zone:<zone>[:<order>[:<step>]] — every card lying in that zone does what it does. How a phase makes cards act rather than waiting for a player to click one: put the rule on a card, put the card in a hidden zone, and have the phase that should run it say so. Ungated — the phase has already decided it is time. The order is the game's to state: naming none acts in the order the cards are in, and "by_column" reads a board left to right, columns first — which is what strikes resolving left to right means on two ranks facing each other. Any other word is refused rather than defaulted. A step names abilities: give one and only the abilities keyed to that word run, so a phase can walk the same zone several times and get an order *between* cards that one pass cannot — every unit works out what it is dealt, then every keyword that reduces a number reduces it, then every unit takes it. Naming none runs every ability. A step wants an order beside it.
_actions.set_active_seat: set_active_seat:<scope> — whoever the scope names becomes the seat whose turn it is. Every other way of naming a seat is settled before the game starts — "mine" and "enemy" are relative to whoever is already up, a seat key is a constant — so this is the only one that reads off what just happened: the trick winner leads the next trick, the attack token holder acts first. The scope names cards and the seat is whose they are, through the same answer "mine" asks, so "owner_of.target" and "target" mean the same thing about an ordinary card. Naming two seats is refused; naming none does nothing. Undo history ends with the turn, as it does at any handover. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.set_priority: set_priority:<scope> — whoever the scope names may act right now, without the turn moving. Priority is who is up inside a response window: the seat answering another player's action, in a window the turn owner's action opened for them. active_seat reads priority over the turn, and "mine", costs, the plays counter and reachability all read active_seat, so this is the whole of letting a card be played out of turn — the reactor pays from their own pool and acts on their own cards while the turn stays where it was. The scope names cards and the seat is whose they are, the same as set_active_seat; naming two seats is refused, naming none does nothing. It does not clear the undo history: the turn has not changed. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.clear_priority: clear_priority — the response window is over, so priority goes back to the turn. active_seat falls back to whose turn it is when nobody holds priority (0), which is every moment outside a window. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.emit: emit:<verb>[:<action>] — announce that something happened, so anybody holding a reaction to that verb may answer it before it stands. The subject is the acting card, which carries the tags a reaction reads ("tagged:gem@event"), so the emitter names nobody who might answer and a chip never has to list what counters it. What is written after the verb is the part that *waits*: "emit:crash:move_target_to:enemy.pile" announces the crash and holds the move until the window closes unanswered, which is the only way to defer half an action when a ravel action list runs to completion. Nothing in the game answers that verb, or the game has no zone tagged "stack": the action after it simply runs now, so an emit costs a game without reactions exactly nothing. For a card announcing its own play, write "emits" on the card or its tag instead.
_actions.counterspell: counterspell — written in a reaction's action: the event it answers does not happen, and the deferred action never runs. **It names no zone.** The stack holds records, never game cards, so a countered card never moved and there is nothing to put back — where it lands was already said by its own "spent". Named for the word every player knows; "cancel" means six other things. The counterpart of emit, and the only spelling that works: "destroy:event" reaches the card the event is *about*, which for a crash is the gem, not the crash.
_actions.each_seat: each_seat:<action> — run one action once per seat, in seat order, with each seat up in turn. The engine knows how many seats there are, and this is what stops content writing the number out: a four-seat deal was four set_active_seat lines and four draws, and adding a fifth player meant editing the phase rather than the players list. Every scope a game writes is already relative to whoever is up, so "mine" does the work and any action at all may be wrapped. Whoever was up is up again when it returns, and no handover happens — the undo history is not cleared and nothing is written to the log, because dealing to everybody is not anybody's turn. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.ready: ready:<scope> — un-spend those cards, the counterpart to the "exhaust" cost. A phase's own actions run when it begins, so this is how a game says *when* being spent wears off rather than taking the engine's round boundary for it.
_actions.reveal: reveal:<card> — conjure a card into the page overlay, where playing it continues the story
_actions.options: options:<source>[:optional] — offer a choice, and open the overlay showing it. The source is either a zone, whose cards name the choices, or a comma-separated list of card keys; either way a fresh card is dealt per choice. The offer remembers the card that asked, and whichever choice is played is played with that card as its target — so a promotion choice says transform:target:queen. Everything left in the offer is cleared when the choice is made. The word "optional" puts a No choice button on the offer, for a question that may go unanswered.
_actions.show: show:<scope>[:optional] — put the REAL cards a scope names into the offer face up and open it, which is how one player reads another’s hand. Each remembers where it came from and goes back there when the offer closes. Choosing one does not play it: the asking card’s chosen block runs instead, with the pick as its target. The word "optional" puts a No choice button on the offer. The scope may say "random.", and then one of them is shown rather than all — "show:random.enemy.hand" is the whole of "reveal a card from their hand", with the seeded RNG picking it.
_actions.reveal_top: reveal_top:<zone> — turn a zone's top card into the page overlay
_actions.resolve_challenge: resolve_challenge — ask the card's challenge and run its pass or its fail
_actions.effect: effect:<name> — play a named visual effect on the acting card, skipped headless
_actions._frozen_while_asking: While an offer is open the phase, the seat and priority are frozen, and next_phase, push_phase, pop_phase, set_active_seat, set_priority, clear_priority and each_seat are refused where they stand. An offer was asked in a phase, of a seat, holding priority: move any of the three and the cards it borrowed have nowhere to come home to, and the player is left with a chooser over a board that has moved on. The refusal is deliberate rather than the engine closing the offer for you — a rule that asks a question and walks away has not said what should happen to it. Put the change in the card's "chosen" list, which runs once the offer has closed; setting a seat or priority BEFORE the show: is fine, since that is the offer's setup rather than a change made underneath it. The validator reports the bad order before the game runs.
_actions.next_phase: next_phase — advance. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.push_phase: push_phase:<phase> — enter a phase and remember where to come back to. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.pop_phase: pop_phase — go back. Refused while an offer is open: see _actions._frozen_while_asking.
_actions.load_game: load_game:<file.json> — switch games. A bare name only: a path or a .. is refused.
_actions.open_game: open_game — ask the player for a game file of their own and play it: a file picker in the browser, a dropped file on the desktop. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is installed. The engine already runs a game handed to it as text — that is how an invite carries its rules to somebody who has never seen the file — so this is only the asking. Silent in a build with no way to ask.
_actions.net_invite: net_invite — build an invite to send somebody
_actions.net_join: net_join — open the box to paste one into
_actions.net_seat: net_seat:<seat> — sit in a chair, or any to give it up
_actions.save_game: save_game:<slot> — write the position to a save, under a plain word the game chooses. The slot says which save, never where it goes: the engine decides that, because a game file can arrive from a stranger. What is written is exactly what a networked opponent would be sent, so there is no second format to keep correct. Refused while a network game is connected, since two people saving one game write two files that both claim to be it.
_actions.load_save: load_save:<slot> — put a saved position back, whichever game it was of: the save names its own file and that file is loaded first. Refused if the game file has changed since it was written, because the same position means something else against different rules. The log comes back with it and the undo history does not, exactly as when a state arrives over the wire.

_engine_tags._what: Tags are the game's own vocabulary and an unknown one is not an error. These are the words the engine itself reads, and they are reserved: a style, a tag with behaviour or a computed tag may not be named after one. A word naming an entry in styles claims a look; one naming an entry in tags claims behaviour.
_engine_tags._on_cards: generate_art (with no asset, draws a shape derived from its key rather than a bare colour), last_acted (the card a player most recently played or activated. Written by the engine, one at a time, and it lingers until the next thing a player does — which is how a rule asks whether something happened *just now*), immutable (scenery: nothing may target it and its template can never be edited), no_undo (playing or picking it clears the undo stack — the choice is final), player (this card is a seat. Stamped by the engine from the players section, not written by hand), token (vanishes when a hand is swept, instead of joining the discard)
_engine_tags._on_zones: optional (nothing here ever has to be played, so a gated card stays gated), refill_when_empty (recreates its contents when the last card leaves), shuffle (shuffled when its contents are created, and on every refill)
_engine_tags._reserved: A zone or tag may never be named self or all, nor any of the quantifiers any, each and random, nor the owner words mine, enemy and anyone. player is deliberately not reserved: it is an ordinary tag a game puts on one card.
_engine_tags._on_phases: discard_hand (leaving it discards the unplayed hand; tokens vanish), keep_hand (a draw_and_play phase opting out of the discard it would otherwise get)
_engine_tags._on_stats: hidden (kept out of the HUD, while cards may still read and change it)
